title: Australian PM Albanese dons Dhaka topi to celebrate Nepal Festival in Sydney - The Kathmandu Post
description: Australian PM Albanese dons Dhaka topi to celebrate Nepal Festival in Sydney  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has praised the Nepali community for its contribution to Australia’s development and its role in enriching the country’s cultural diversity.

Albanese attended the Nepal Festival organised by the Non-Resident Nepali Association (NRNA) Australia for the first time, praising the community’s contribution to Australian society. He was welcomed at the event with a traditional Nepali Dhaka topi and khada scarf.

In an upbeat mood, Albanese said Australia was a multicultural country and that Nepalis had made an important contribution to its overall development. He also extended Tihar greetings to those attending the festival.

The NRNA Australia has been organising the Nepal Festival for the past two decades to promote Nepali art, culture and tourism. This was the first time an Australian prime minister had attended an event organised by the Nepali community.

The NRNA Australia organised the Nepal Festival on Saturday at Darling Harbour, a popular tourist destination in Sydney. Narayan Khadka/TKP

During his address, Albanese also mentioned Nepali security officer Bikash Bharati, who was recently honoured for courageously carrying out his duties.

The prime minister expressed condolences to those who lost their lives in the floods and landslides that hit Nepal in August, and said Australia stood with the country in its relief and reconstruction efforts.

Albanese later took to social media to say he had celebrated Tihar with the Nepali community.

Chris Minns, premier of New South Wales, also attended the festival and praised Nepali art and culture.

The NRNA Australia organised the Nepal Festival on Saturday at Darling Harbour, a popular tourist destination in Sydney. Organisers said thousands of people attended.

The festival opened with a Nepal parade showcasing traditional dress and culture. Stalls offering Nepali food and featuring businesses were also set up.

The event drew not only members of the Nepali community but also a significant number of local residents.

The NRNA Australia holds the Nepal Festival every two years to promote Nepal’s art, culture and tourism.

title: Analysis: How many times will Nepal resettle its disaster-affected? - Eco-Business
description: Analysis: How many times will Nepal resettle its disaster-affected?  Eco-Business
publisher.title: Eco-Business
full_article:
Additionally, 2018 research covering Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Kathmandu districts found gaps in Nepal’s geo-hazard assessment methodology and a lack of precision. For instance, it did not capture new or changing risk in the area, with the assessment confined to a single date. The research also noted that following the NRA’s assessments in those districts, there were no clear relocation plans, nor any policy attention on livelihood opportunities at new sites.

In fact, just last year, a government report was written after a smaller flood on Trishuli River, which Khalte sat along the banks of, reported Nepali outlet OnlineKhabar. It found that construction along the river was at risk, and identified Khalte as one of the settlements at high risk of flooding, the outlet noted. Earlier this month, local officials told the Kathmandu Post they had been preparing to move Khalte’s residents to a new site when the 26 August floods struck.

A recurring issue

The flood-affected districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading are at constant risk, and comprehensive studies are needed before developing settlements in those areas, Khum Narayan Paudayal, a geology professor at Tribhuvan University, told news outlet Lokaantar. He added that resettlement should not be allowed in flood-affected areas just because there is land left.

But this pattern of impermanent resettlement extends far beyond these districts.

Earlier this year, research into two villages deemed unsafe by geo-hazard assessments undertaken after the earthquake was published in the journal World Development. Landslide debris could fall onto Lampat in Sindhupalchok district, the researchers found. While Bosimpa, in Dolakha district, was “located on a large unstable slope”. Despite these warnings, in 2023 the researchers found residents living in houses just several kilometres away, some built with government subsidies.

They also found that, in the settlements intended to replace both villages, over half of the houses stood empty. The new sites lacked farmland, adequate infrastructure, or the water and electricity residents had been promised.

Construction costs routinely exceeded government subsidies, driving many households into debt. In Rasuwa, the 2021 research article found residents expected their new settlement to serve only as a home during the monsoon season, since their economic and social ties remained in their original villages.

They did not move far away from disaster either. Floods along Melamchi River inundated Sindhupalchok district in June 2021, killing at least 25 people and impacting hundreds of families.

Half a year later, survivors who did not proactively move were still awaiting a resettlement decision as officials lacked the risk data needed to determine where rebuilding was safe, Dialogue Earth reported. It noted that local authorities requested a comprehensive study of the whole watershed, but never received one.

Resettlements in Nepal are challenging because landslide and flood risks in the country’s mountainous terrain are not rooted in one location, the World Development researchers note. They continue evolving years after the event that first exposed them.

What makes 2026 different

Though some improvements have been made to disaster response since 2015, several aspects have remained slow to develop.

In the aftermath of the August floods, it remains unclear which authority will be overseeing resettlement.

In 2015, Nepal built the entirely new NRA from scratch. It had a fixed-term mandate focused strictly on earthquake recovery, and its own workforce to do it.

This time, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) led the Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment, having taken over the NRA’s work when it closed in 2021. No dedicated post-floods reconstruction body has been announced, meaning resettlement could compete with the NDRRMA’s other work.

The government’s needs assessment capabilities have improved since 2015. In September, the NDRRMA’s rapid assessment was published just over two weeks after the flood, largely produced from satellite and drone data. It identified priority recovery requirements, giving NGOs, international partners and the government lead time in designing aid packages. In 2015, the government only released a Post-Disaster Needs Assessment, albeit more in-depth, roughly two months after the earthquake.

But in the aftermath of the August floods, the plight of landless and undocumented households appears similar to a decade prior, when many were not counted and supported in recovery efforts.

In September, two ministries wrote a bill to amend two land laws. This would require the state to arrange alternative settlements for landless people living in high-risk locations including riverbanks, forests, road rights-of-way and other disaster-prone land. Khalte’s residents have fit that description for years, but there was no such legal obligation to help them. The bill remains in draft form.

This year, with the legislative amendment pending, those are the households that appear most likely to be left out again.

After 2015, ownership of homestead land became a prerequisite for households to receive the main housing reconstruction grant given by the NRA. By late 2016, about 13 per cent of eligible households in districts worst hit by the earthquakes were still unable to sign the grant agreement as they lacked ownership papers.

This year, authors of the August floods’ rapid assessment acknowledge that no household survey, key informant interviews or structured community consultations were carried out for it. The assessment also states the housing, land and property concerns of tenants, landless households and people without documentation were not comprehensively examined.

There are a few things a resettlement site in 2026 must get right to be considered safe, permanent and viable in the long term. An independent geological safety assessment must be completed before anyone is moved there, not years later, as in the case of Khalte.

Land tenure issues and financial arrangements must be settled before construction begins, so families are not left occupying informal ground indefinitely, like many of Khalte’s residents have been for the past decade. Long-term livelihood opportunities have to be designed into the site from the outset.

The 41-year-old resident’s account is proof of this failure. He has now been moved, or left to move himself, three times. Each time, a formal plan for where he should go next either arrived years too late or not at all.

title: They have gone 10 weeks without answers. Will these families ever know what happened to loved ones missing after Nepal’s floods? - The Guardian
description: They have gone 10 weeks without answers. Will these families ever know what happened to loved ones missing after Nepal’s floods?  The Guardian
publisher.title: The Guardian
full_article:
E very day, Nikhila Agastya answers more questions from her two children: has she heard anything about their father? Is he with anyone? Is it snowing in Kathmandu? Is he cold, and does he have warm clothing? Will he come home? The answer is: probably not.

“They know that [their] father is missing,” Nikhila says. “And they are still looking for him. They always wait; every day they wait for him. They won’t give up, they think he will come home.”

Her husband, Gopi Agastya, had travelled from Sydney to Nepal to go on a pilgrimage with the Isha Foundation when a flood hit on 26 August. He did not return home.

It has been 10 weeks since the catastrophic floods wiped away whole villages, reaching settlements as high as 82 metres above the river level.

The number of dead has risen to 1,459. Another 5,285 people are unaccounted for. More than 700 of them are foreigners – including 34 Australians – with families who have had no answers for 10 long weeks.

Nikhila last spoke to her husband the morning of the floods, before he entered the immigration centre at the border with Tibet. Gopi was excited about coming home – he missed their two girls, aged 13 and 7, and wanted to eat a home-cooked meal with them. The two parents planned to take the children on a cruise when he returned.

View image in fullscreen Gopi Agastya was on a pilgrimage in Nepal when the floods hit

The days that followed are now a blur to Nikhila. She travelled to India to be with family, while a friend whose husband was also missing went to Nepal and filtered any small pieces of information back: the border was still inaccessible; the Isha Foundation was trying to get in; families were putting up posters of loved ones on hospital walls in a desperate hope they would be found.

Nikhila sent images to Australia’s department of foreign affairs – of the shoes he would be wearing, his jacket, beanie, sun goggles – anything that could help identify him.

“He’s a very lovable person. Everyone likes him. He had good friends. I recently spoke to a friend of his, and he said Gopi is not just his name; Gopi is a brand.”

He was also the sole breadwinner of the family. The pair married 15 years ago and moved to Australia: he worked in IT for a major supermarket chain and she focused on their children. But Nikhila is now looking for work, with a government parenting payment nowhere near what Gopi was earning.

Amid these pressures, she can’t help but hope Gopi might come home.

No answers

Every morning for the last 10 weeks, Linda Govender has sent a WhatsApp message to her daughter. And every day, she receives no reply.

Her daughter, Terricia, was in an immigration centre when the floods hit. Now her mother is running a global campaign on behalf of the families of missing foreigners.

“The uncertainty is unbearable,” Govender says from South Africa. “You wake up every morning hoping for news, checking your phone, reading messages and wondering whether today will finally be the day somebody has an answer.”

View image in fullscreen ‘For the families, the disaster does not end’ … Linda Govender and her daughter Terricia

Govender travelled to the flood zone in the days after, hiring a helicopter with other families to search by air. She returned home to Isipingo Beach, south of Durban, with no answers.

Realising many others were in the same situation, she then set up Global Voices for the Missing – an online community where families can share information and advocate. She says they want Nepal’s government to keep searching to find the whereabouts of the deceased and to maintain regular communication with affected families.

“We understand that difficult decisions have to be made following a natural disaster,” she says. “But families deserve to know that every reasonable avenue has been explored.

“For the families, the disaster does not end. We are still waking up every morning wondering where our loved ones are. We are still waiting for information.”

View image in fullscreen Terricia, who is still missing in Nepal

Soon after the floods, the government of Nepal sought to help speed up that information and set up DNA testing that could match families with the remains of their loved ones.

More than 2,000 people have given their DNA. At the start of October, only 112 bodies were transferred back to families. The process is slow and the backlog is large.

Governments around the world have also been working with their Nepali and Tibetan counterparts to begin the official process of issuing death certificates.

‘We keep continuing’

In the days after the floods, families from around the world rushed to Kathmandu. They hired 4WDs to take them as far as they could into the flood zones, they spoke to embassy officials and politicians, they visited the hospitals, sticking images of their loved ones up on the walls.

Last month, Nepal officially ended the search-and-rescue operation, moving into the “search-and-rehabilitation phase”, according to Phanindra Paudel, the chief of the National Emergency Operation Centre.

Authorities would no longer actively search for bodies but would recover any remains, property or other valuables found during the rehabilitation process, he said.

For hundreds of families around the world, waiting for any news, it was a blow.

Those who took it upon themselves to search for loved ones have not found it easy. Nepal’s government is still trying to clear debris to get up to the border with China, with many roads still closed. Nepal has said rebuilding will cost close to US$4.78bn (A$6.93bn) and has called for greater support for that mammoth undertaking, which will take years.

Thousands were displaced – now living in centres, tents, monasteries, or with extended family. They do not know when they will be able to return home.

View image in fullscreen ‘It was scary, it was bad’ … mud covering properties after the floods in Trishuli, Nuwakot district. Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters

Sagar Pandey is the chief executive of the Himalayan Glacier Company. His company had 47 people – including 15 Australians – in tour groups in Nepal’s north when the floods hit. His brother was guiding one of them.

“It was scary, it was bad,” Pandey says. “But now, people are trying to overcome; people are trying to continue their lives in a new way.

“It’s been really hard; they can’t forget, but also people don’t have a choice.”

Nepal has been reeling from the floods, which hit during one of the country’s peak tourist times. Adding to the impact is the fact that overseas visitors are no longer coming. Last year, the country welcomed more than 1.1 million visitors, contributing about 6.7% to the gross domestic product (GDP): now, the number has dropped off. Pandey has lost almost 80% of his usual bookings for this time of year.

“We have the missing guides’ children we have to support, to pay for the future for their schools. So we keep continuing.”

‘How do I not crumble?’ Loved ones of Australians missing in Nepal-Tibet floods fear others are turning away Read more

Anita Cook is among that small group of visitors returning to Nepal. She owns iNeeta cafe, a world away from the Himalayas, and one of the few shops in the small Australian town of Moyhu, Victoria. She has been to Nepal twice, and is now taking her two boys to hike the Annapurna circuit.

“Once you’ve been there, it just really leaves a really strong impact on you,” she says. “The way these people live, they’ve got nothing, but they’re the happiest people on the earth and they would do anything, anything to help you.”

Her cafe is full of plants she is selling to raise funds, while the local pub is contributing $1 for every parma sold. She is taking $12,000 the small community has raised and putting it straight into the hands of the guides she knows well – they’ve lost families, are connected to the community and she trusts they can give the money to the right people. But she says the best thing she can do is get on a plane and trek.

“[When it happened] I would have jumped on a plane and went straight away. But we are going now, because trekking in the mountains is the bread and butter of all these people.”

‘I just hope’

For people who went missing at the border, the process has been harder – determining which country they were in when the flood hit has been difficult.

The family of Renee Spry, a woman from the Sunshine Coast, have been waiting while this process happens along with the 49 other families from her group.

“There was some confusion about where they were lost,” Renee’s sister Jacinta says.

“But at the end of it, Nepal agreed that they were on the Nepalese side, and they would be the ones who would be trying to issue death certificates.”

View image in fullscreen Renee Spry is still missing. Her sister says the uncertainty has been the hardest thing for the family

A fortnight after the flood, Renee’s husband and two daughters travelled to Nepal. They could not get to the border area, but provided DNA samples, put pictures of her up and visited the temples she had gone to before her pilgrimage. They raised the money to travel through GoFundMe and donated $10,000 to the Emergency Action Alliance.

“They were prepared they might go there and not really get any answers,” she says. “I still think it was a therapeutic thing that they did it.”

Jacinta says “it is a funny kind of grief”: to lose someone and have no answers, no physical representation that they are gone. “The uncertainty has probably been the hardest bit,” she says. “Feeling just a bit hopeless about it, feeling removed and a long way away.”

The family want people to keep paying attention to Nepal – on the redevelopment and also the increasing disasters the climate crisis is causing in the small country.

“If you were talking to Renee, she would say there are all these people still trying to live there,” Spry says. “In this ongoing danger, in this evolving climate catastrophe.

“She would be worried about them. She would be like, ‘what’s everyone doing about this?’”

For many families, like Nikhila’s, the lack of information has not extinguished their hope that, one day, their loved ones will be found.

“I always feel like that,” she says. “I just hope, still, something, he might be there, somewhere. I just hope.”

title: UN expert urges Nepal to revive stalled transitional justice process - The Kathmandu Post
description: UN expert urges Nepal to revive stalled transitional justice process  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
A United Nations human rights expert has urged Nepal to make transitional justice a national priority, calling on the government to expedite appointments to the two transitional justice commissions and revive a process that has made little progress nearly two decades after the end of the decade-long armed conflict.

Bernard Duhaime, the UN Special Rapporteur on the promotion of truth, justice, reparation and guarantees of non-recurrence, made the call as Nepal prepares to mark the 20th anniversary of the Comprehensive Peace Accord, signed on November 21, 2006, which formally ended the Maoist insurgency.

There have been delays despite national and international concerns on forming those two commissions related to Nepal's transitional justice process agreed in 2006 between the government and the then Maoist rebels.

“Since the Accord was signed in 2006, several transitional justice initiatives have been launched, yet progress has remained slow,” Duhaime said in a statement issued by the UN Human Rights Office.

He said the formation of a new administration earlier this year had created an opportunity to strengthen governance and reinvigorate the transitional justice agenda, adding that the opportunity must not be missed.

Duhaime urged the government to swiftly appoint commissioners to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission and the Commission of Investigation on Enforced Disappeared Persons so that the two bodies could resume their work.

He also called on the authorities to engage meaningfully and robustly with international human rights mechanisms and bodies to fulfil Nepal's commitments to justice, accountability and human rights.

The UN expert expressed regret that he could not undertake his planned country visit to Nepal this year. He said he would continue working with the government to identify alternative dates, describing a visit as an important opportunity to deepen engagement and support efforts to advance transitional justice and protect victims' rights.

Nepal's transitional justice process has remained stalled amid political disagreements, legal and institutional challenges, and delays in appointing officials to the two commissions. Thousands of conflict victims and families of the disappeared continue to wait for truth, justice and reparation.

The two commissions have been without office-bearers since the government removed their previous leadership through an ordinance in May this year. The delay in appointing new officials has also affected the planned visit of the UN special rapporteur.

title: David Warner's Fielding Gaffe Leads to 5-Run Penalty in Nepal Premier League - Ratopati
description: David Warner's Fielding Gaffe Leads to 5-Run Penalty in Nepal Premier League  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. In the third edition of the Nepal Premier League (NPL), an unusual fielding by former Australian captain and aggressive batter David Warner resulted in the opposing team being penalized 5 runs.

During fielding, Warner used a handkerchief to catch the ball, after which the umpire awarded the opposing team a 5-run penalty. According to cricket rules, players are not allowed to stop or catch the ball with the help of any external object or equipment not in their hands. Therefore, Warner's action was considered against the rules.

According to Article 28.2 of the International Cricket Council (ICC) Cricket Rules, a fielder can stop or catch the ball using any part of their body. However, deliberately stopping or catching the ball using an object other than the body is considered illegal fielding.

According to this rule, if such a mistake occurs, the umpire must immediately declare the ball 'dead' and award 5 penalty runs to the batting team. In addition, runs completed by the batter and runs where both batters have crossed each other at the time of the mistake will also be added. Such a ball is not counted in the over.

This incident occurred on Saturday in a match between Kathmandu Gurkhas and Lumbini Lions at the TU International Cricket Ground in Kirtipur.

In this match, Kathmandu, batting first, scored 160 runs for the loss of 8 wickets in their allotted 20 overs. David Warner scored 66 runs off 50 balls for Kathmandu, while Sahil Patel added 38 runs off 36 balls. The two shared a 104-run partnership for the first wicket.

Warner's incident highlights how even seemingly normal actions in cricket can be against the rules, leading to teams having to face penalties.

Meanwhile, Kathmandu defeated Lumbini by 36 runs.

title: Deuba expresses confidence in court verdict on Nepali Congress legitimacy dispute - Khabarhub
description: Deuba expresses confidence in court verdict on Nepali Congress legitimacy dispute  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Former Nepali Congress (NC) President Sher Bahadur Deuba has expressed confidence that the court will deliver justice in the ongoing dispute over the party’s official legitimacy, maintaining that his faction represents the legitimate Nepali Congress.

Addressing the Kathmandu District Convention organised by his faction in the capital on Saturday, Deuba said the judicial process would ultimately establish the party’s legitimate leadership.

He also accused the Gagan Thapa Nepali Congress of engaging in large-scale financial irregularities in connection with the party’s legitimacy dispute. Referring to the recent Inam Sapkota case, he claimed that it had further exposed financial manipulation surrounding the issue.

Deuba also announced that he would not seek another term as party president at the upcoming general convention, signalling his intention to focus on strengthening the organisation and contributing to the country in other capacities.

Stating that he had received much from the Nepali Congress over the years, Deuba said he now wanted to move forward by bringing everyone together and ensuring wider participation within the party.

He emphasised the need for unity and collective efforts to strengthen the party as it navigates the ongoing leadership and legitimacy dispute.

title: Rethinking Nepal’s Development Finance - The Rising Nepal
description: Rethinking Nepal’s Development Finance  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
The devastating floods of the Bhotekoshi, the Kali Gandaki and the Budhi Gandaki River corridors during late August to early October 2026 in the Himalayan Mountains have warned us about the vulnerability of Nepal’s development finance model. These floods, possibly triggered by climate-induced tragedies, have swept away strategic bridges and people's houses and severely damaged infrastructure. This is not the exception, as Nepal has been witnessing similar disasters over the last few years.

Together, these cyclical disasters have been warning the authorities to rethink the development and public investment model the country has been adopting for the last three or more decades. There is a fundamental ambiguity about our capacity to finance infrastructure, which was undermined in considering, informing, and managing the geographical and climatic risks to which the country is vulnerable. The fundamental infrastructures such as roads, bridges, business corridors, human settlements and hydropower projects remain vulnerable to extreme climatic floods, landslides and sudden changes in river behaviour.

Risk planning

The very preliminary assessment by the government estimates around Rs. 400 billion in asset damage and economic losses from the August Bhotekoshi disaster alone. In the meantime, the Kali Gandaki and Budhi Gandaki rivers repeatedly washed away several strategic infrastructures and means of livelihood. Here the fundamental question is not simply how quickly we can rebuild the damaged public properties but why our public investments continue to be exposed to such devastating risks in the first place.

The vital question is whether we should keep investing public resources in the same development patterns that again and again expose people, infrastructure and public finances to intolerable risks. Now the time has come that the nation needs an immediate shift in both infrastructure planning and development finance.

Over time, the country’s development priorities have been severely guided by political promises, election consciousness and the undue charm of large infrastructure projects. Often it is observed that the roads, bridges and other physical structures with very little value addition for the economy are counted as symbols of progress and political achievement. However, vulnerability assessment, antagonistic climate risks, river dynamics and long-term liabilities have not always received the attention they deserve.

It is obvious that the country needs better connectivity, reliable energy, resilient settlements and productive infrastructure, but it should be linked to employment, income and socioeconomic transformation of the community. Nepal, a country with steep slopes, fragile geological formations and unpredictable river systems, cannot rely only on conventional tools of development planning and investment modelling.

The burning issue of climate change has been complicating the planning and budgeting process as illustrated by the latest climate-induced disasters. It says how a hazard originating in a remote mountain catchment can cascade downstream, destroying infrastructure and livelihoods far beyond its point of origin. Such events warn the planner why risk-informed planning and budgeting are the most resilient strategic infrastructure networks.

Development economics

Flaws of the development model cannot be explained by technical limitations alone. It has a strong association with the political economy of public investment, procurement and natural-resource management. Economists believe that large public investments create opportunities for augmented economic activities and promote private sectors. However, it has been a common practice that the selection of strategic projects followed by the financial closure, procurement, construction and environmental regulation were often guided by political influence, resulting in conflicts of interest and rent-seeking incentives.

It was an open secret that the nexus among the political actors, public officials, regulators and business inflated project costs, compromised environmental safeguards and distorted engineering standards. Such a nexus resulted in a poorly regulated extraction of natural resources that was responsible for changing river channels, destabilising riverbanks and weakening nearby infrastructure.

In the meantime, politically exposed individuals and businesses knowingly occupy risky locations because of land market incentives and weak enforcement due to undue favours from the leadership. It would be unfair to attribute every incident to political economy, but we must acknowledge that the unchecked nexus creates risks for emergency services, public infrastructure and the wider economy.

The distorted development finance impacts far beyond the cost of reconstruction, affecting public revenue, household income, private investment and the government’s ability to finance essential services. When roads and bridges are destroyed, transport and trade are disrupted, and associated revenue declines, which in turn affects livelihoods, raises insurance claims and drags the economy into recession.

In response, public funds get diverted towards emergency relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction, creating a vicious cycle of fiscal burden. The government opted for debt financing to build infrastructure, but the misguided risk management and political-economy nexus leave these investments vulnerable to destruction, making new borrowing compulsory to restore what was lost. Meanwhile, debt-servicing obligations continue, even when the assets financed by borrowing are no longer delivering their expected economic and social returns.

Nepal cannot sustain such a vicious cycle, and the debt, which is supposed to finance productive assets, cannot repeatedly fund the replacement of infrastructure whose risks were ignored in the first place. This is creating a 'Double Shoulders' challenge for the present government, i.e. mobilise the finance for reconstruction and recovery while protecting the public budget from the recurrence of avoidable losses.

Opportunity for reforms

The present government has an opportunity to address this fundamental problem of development finance. Recovery is a pragmatic tool for rethinking development policies, institutional practices and investment modelling to avoid recurring loss and damage.

First of all, an evidence-based review of engineering codes and infrastructure standards for high-risk areas, with a flexible clause that allows such standards to be periodically updated with evolving evidence. Second, climate-induced disaster risk screening should be made mandatory for major public infrastructure investments.

Thirdly, risk-based zoning of river corridors with strong regulation is essential, especially for the areas that are exposed to exceptional flood and climate-induced hazards. In case of unavoidable risks, critical infrastructure and human settlements should be restricted or relocated with practical alternatives.

Fourthly, river-based material extraction must be governed by science-based limits rather than short-term revenue considerations. Finally, indigenous knowledge and skills should be institutionalised with proper testing and documentation in the development model.

Policy and planning reforms alone will not work unless Nepal rethinks how it mobilises and invests development finance. Tax-based budgets and debt financing are already under pressure from competing demands for infrastructure, social protection, universal health, education and unforeseen economic recovery.

It is high time for the government to implement a diversified framework for alternative development finance. However, alternative development finance must not become another route for contingent liabilities to invest in poorly appraised projects. As the conventional Public-Private Partnerships (PPP) could not work as expected, it requires rigorous value-for-money assessments and transparent disclosure of the government’s long-term financial commitments.

Investments in early-warning systems, river monitoring, hazard mapping, resilient infrastructure and planned relocation may not produce the immediate political visibility like a road or bridge, but their economic returns can be substantial when measured against avoided losses.

Development financing should be evaluated by whether such investments help reduce vulnerability, ease livelihoods, improve public services and generate sustainable economic returns.

The latest floods gave a painful signal that risk does not respect administrative boundaries, political promises or budget constraints. A bridge built without adequate consideration of flood risk, a settlement established in an unsafe corridor, can impose costs on generations of taxpayers. Thus, the challenge of development finance is about changing the investment incentives and institutions that shape public investment.

Political leaders should think beyond the volume of budget sanctioned for the physical structures that they will lay foundation stones for. The government must now stop the recurring cycle of construction, destruction and reconstruction by pursuing prudent public accountability and financial sustainability.

Public officials should dare to enforce scientific standards and to resist undue political pressure. Contractors must follow responsible business practices in compliance with quality and legal standards, whereas communities should be empowered to scrutinise the projects' dashboards and whittle down the violations. Most importantly, planners should dare to accept that disaster resilience is not an additional cost but rather a precondition for protecting development gains.





(The author is an applied economist with experience in economic policy and development research.)

title: Five Books by Literary Figure Moti Shobha Shrestha Launched - Ratopati
description: Five Books by Literary Figure Moti Shobha Shrestha Launched  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. Five works by literary figure Moti Shobha Shrestha written in Nepali, Nepal Bhasa, and English have been launched simultaneously.

The five works were launched at a program held in Kathmandu on Saturday, presided over by former Finance Minister and literary figure Shankar Prasad Koirala, with former Chief Minister and literary figure Bimal Koirala as the chief guest, and Chairman of the Nepali Sahitya Sraṣṭā Samaj and literary figure ShriOm Shrestha as the special guest.

Among the launched works are two books in Nepali, two in Nepal Bhasa, and one in English. The Nepali language collection of stories 'Sapana Ko Udan' and the travelogue 'Yatra Ko Veg: Anubhutiko Samveg' have been launched.

Similarly, the Nepal Bhasa collection of stories 'Takyangu Suka' and the novella 'Rangi Changi Swan Chhayapiyatgu Keb', and the English language novella 'Mother Who Named Me Satya' have been launched.

At the program, senior storyteller and novelist Bhagirathi Shrestha and literary figure and artist Gyanendra Biwash discussed the launched books. Other distinguished literary figures were also present at the program.

Moti Shobha's collection of stories 'Sapana Ko Udan' includes 38 stories. The stories, based on human life, human emotions, love, nature, and contemporary themes, cover events and contexts seen in daily life. Positive thinking and messages are presented in the stories with simple language and diverse subject matter.

'Yatra Ko Veg: Anubhutiko Samveg' is the author's first travelogue. The book describes the environment, lifestyle, historical significance, art, culture, and natural beauty of various places around the world. The experiences of joy and sorrow, unforgettable events, and contexts encountered during the journey are also included in the book.

The Nepal Bhasa published 'Takyangu Suka' includes 60 stories that highlight various aspects of human life. This is a Nepal Bhasa translated version of the author's previously published work.

Similarly, the Nepal Bhasa novella 'Rangi Changi Swan Chhayapiyatgu Keb' focuses on the changing family structure, joint families, and inter-caste harmony. The English language novella 'Mother Who Named Me Satya' is also a translation of a previously published Nepali work. It presents the problem of child labor hidden in society and the importance of proper protection for children.

Shrestha, who has been actively writing literature since 2078 BS, has previously published five novellas and two collections of stories in Nepali. Among these, four novellas and one collection of stories have been translated and published in Nepal Bhasa, and one novella has been published in English.

At the program, in recognition of her contribution to Nepal Bhasa and literature, Shrestha was honored by Mangalman Shakya, Chairman of the Nepal Bhasa Foundation.

Shrestha, who served in government service for a long time, retired from the post of Joint Secretary at the Ministry of Labor and Transport. She is currently active in literary activities, associated with various literary organizations.

title: Nepal releases names of 2,465 missing after August 26 floods; 171 foreigners among them - The New Indian Express

full_article:
Nepal on Saturday released details of 2,294 nationals from 32 districts and 171 foreign nationals from seven countries who went missing after devastating floods struck the Himalayan nation on August 26.

The announcement comes a month after the government called off its 40-day search-and-rescue operation for victims of the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods, which claimed at least 1,455 lives and left 5,285 people missing, according to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).

The authority clarified that the list includes only those whose missing status has been verified by the respective District Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Committees. No further details were available about the remaining missing persons who were not included in Saturday's list.

The disaster management authority has asked individuals listed as missing, or their immediate family members, to submit a claim within seven days if they are subsequently found to be alive or located.

Rasuwa district accounts for the highest number of missing Nepali nationals, with 1,538 people, according to the NDRRMA list.

The authority has also published details of 171 missing foreign nationals from seven countries, excluding India. The list is available on its official website.

Of the missing foreign nationals, 54 are from Malaysia and Ukraine, 33 from Australia, 11 from Russia, nine from South Korea, eight from Germany and two from Italy.

The NDRRMA said it had not yet received a verified list of missing Indian nationals from the Indian Embassy.

The list of missing Nepali nationals was compiled based on recommendations from local governments in the areas where the individuals had their permanent residences. It was subsequently approved by the respective District Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Committees.

Information on missing foreign nationals was obtained through the Department of Consular Services and diplomatic missions based in Nepal or those designated to oversee the country, the authority said.

The NDRRMA said it would issue a revised notice after receiving further information from district administration offices in the 32 affected districts and the relevant diplomatic missions.

Nepal called off its 40-day search-and-rescue operation on October 5 and shifted its focus to rehabilitation and reconstruction in the affected areas.

The flash floods originated near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastating towns and villages across northern and central Nepal.

The Bhotekoshi River, which flows south from the Himalayan border region, carried the floodwaters downstream, sweeping away houses, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaging several hydropower projects.

title: Nepal eyes $2bn financial package, fresh air routes during PM Balen Shah's upcoming India visit - WION

full_article:
New Delhi: Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah is expected to visit India from 22 to 24 November, with Kathmandu seeking new aviation routes and a financial package of around $2 billion.

The three-day trip will be Shah’s first bilateral visit since he took office in March 2026, following elections that brought his Rastriya Swatantra Party to power after Gen Z-led protests. He earlier travelled to New York for the UN General Assembly, but this will be his first official engagement with a neighbouring country. The last Nepalese prime ministerial visit to India was by Pushpa Kamal Dahal “Prachanda” in June 2023, making this the first such trip in more than three years.

Preparations advanced after Indian Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri’s two-day visit to Kathmandu on 4-5 November. FS Misri met Prime Minister Shah, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal and Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai. Discussions covered connectivity, trade, energy, development cooperation and people-to-people ties. A joint statement noted progress on bilateral initiatives and possible outcomes for the forthcoming high-level visit. Shah thanked India for its rapid response to destructive flash floods in August 2026 and described the planned trip as one he hoped would be “result-oriented.”

Nepal has prioritised additional air-entry routes through Indian airspace. Nepali officials want better access for the international airports. Most international flights currently enter via a single congested corridor over Simara. Kathmandu has long sought points near Janakpur, Bhairahawa and Nepalgunj. Progress on these routes is seen as essential to linking the airports more effectively with Indian cities and boosting tourism and trade.

Kathmandu, Nov 7: The Nepal Electricity Authority has estimated that the peak demand of power on the day of Laxmi Puja this year would be around 1,700 megawatts.

The NEA stated that it would ensure an adequate supply of electricity on the day of Laxmi Puja. Executive Director of the NEA, Dirghayu Kumar Shrestha, said power produced in the country is sufficient to meet the estimated demand of the electricity on the day of Laxmi Puja.

During the period, electricity generation is projected to reach around 2,500 megawatts. He claimed that the sufficient amount of electricity would be available to make power supply smooth as power production exceeds than domestic demand.

The NEA has made special preparation to ensure reliable, regular and quality power supply to consumers on the occasion of Tihar and Chhath festival.

Chiefs of all concerned offices have been directed to make all necessary preparation to avoid any disruption in power supply during festivals, Shrestha added.

The NEA also asked the office chiefs to regularly pick up telephone calls received at no-light service to address the complaints about power supply. (RSS)
